title: FRM Foundations, Lesson 11: Board-level risk governance - who does the CRO report to
subtitle: Why the chief risk officer's reporting line matters more than the content of the report
whyItMatters: Almost every major risk management failure had a risk function that saw the problem and raised it. What was missing was not information but power: the person carrying the bad news reported to the person who benefited from ignoring it. The governance structure decides whether a warning arrives.
openingQuestion: A bank's chief risk officer reports directly to the CEO, whose bonus is tied to the year's profit. What is the biggest structural risk here?
openingOptions: The CRO will lack the business information to assess the positions correctly
The person who has to say no depends on that person for pay and position
The board will receive far too many detailed risk reports
The cost of running the risk function will rise considerably
explanation: The problem is not capability or information but incentives. When the CRO reports only to the CEO, blocking a profitable transaction means contradicting the person who decides their pay and their position. Post-2008 governance standards therefore require the CRO to have a direct reporting line to the board's Risk Committee, and the appointment or removal of the CRO must go through the board rather than being within the executive's sole authority.

diagram.label: The board - sets risk appetite, approves the framework
The board's Risk Committee - where the CRO reports directly
The CRO and the risk function - second line of defence, independent of the business
Internal audit - third line, reporting to the Audit Committee

realWorldExample.company: The collapses of major financial institutions
realWorldExample.description: In many of these failures, the internal minutes show the risk function raising the issue months before the loss surfaced. The warning was downgraded to a recommendation, then to a note, then vanished before reaching the board - not because anyone deleted it, but because every intermediate layer had a reasonable motive to soften it a little.

quiz.question: Why does the CRO need a direct reporting line to the board's Risk Committee?
options: So that the CRO can personally approve every large trading limit in the bank
So that the board has real-time position data available at all times
So that the executive team has a smaller volume of reports to process
So that a warning reaches the decision point without passing through its subject
quiz.explanation: The reporting line is the mechanism that protects independence. If every warning has to travel through the executive, the person with an interest in keeping a profitable activity running is also the person deciding which warnings continue upward - and they need not act in bad faith at all, only keep finding that it is not yet serious enough to escalate. Approving limits is an executive task the CRO should not hold, and a board that receives raw position data has replaced governance with operations.

quiz.question: In the three lines of defence model, who is the first line?
options: The business unit itself, where risk is created and taken on
The risk management function, independent of the business
Internal audit, reporting to the board's Audit Committee
The state regulator, supervising the firm from outside it entirely
quiz.explanation: The first line is the party that creates the risk and therefore owns it - the head of the business, not the risk function. Getting this wrong produces a culture in which risk is seen as the risk department's job, and the second line becomes a gatekeeper to be circumvented rather than a partner. The risk function and internal audit are the second and third lines respectively, and the regulator sits outside the model altogether: supervision is not a line of defence the firm operates.

quiz.question: Which responsibility belongs to the board rather than to the executive?
options: Setting the daily trading limits for each individual desk
Approving the risk appetite statement for the whole firm
Operating the real-time position monitoring infrastructure
Performing the validation of derivatives pricing models used
quiz.explanation: The board decides how much risk the institution is prepared to take - a strategic choice belonging to the owners. The executive translates that statement into specific limits and operates within the framework. A board that sets desk-level limits has stepped into management, while an executive that sets its own appetite has stepped into the owners' authority. Monitoring systems and model validation are operational and technical work respectively, and neither is a board function.

quiz.question: Scenario: The risk function and a desk head disagree about a large position. Which mechanism handles it correctly?
options: Let the risk function decide, since it is the second line of defence
Let the desk head decide, since they understand the market better
Take it up to the level with authority under the escalation process
Suspend the position until the two sides can agree between themselves
quiz.explanation: Disagreement between the first and second lines is not an incident but a sign that the system is working. What matters is having an escalation process written in advance, stating who decides at what level - because if the process has to be negotiated in the middle of the argument, whichever side has more power will win. Handing the decision automatically to either party removes the tension the model is built to create, and waiting for agreement lets delay decide.

quiz.question: Why does the independence of internal audit require that it not report to the executive?
options: Because it lacks sufficient expertise in the business operations
Because it needs approval authority over departmental budgets
Because it only works at the request of the supervisory authority
Because it has to be able to assess the executive team as well
quiz.explanation: The third line checks whether the other two are doing their jobs, and the executive falls within the scope of that check. A function reporting to the very party it assesses no longer provides assurance - which is why internal audit reports to the board's Audit Committee. Nor does it hold budget authority over anyone, since that would make it a decision maker inside the process it reviews, and its work plan comes from the committee rather than from the supervisor.

practicePrompt.question: The CRO reports to the CEO, and the CRO's bonus is tied to the bank's overall profit. Where is the governance problem?
options: Warnings are blocked exactly where they need hearing, and the incentives point the wrong way
There is no problem, since the CEO carries the ultimate responsibility
It only matters if the CRO has actually been pressed to change a conclusion
The problem is the bonus; the reporting line itself is entirely fine
practicePrompt.explanation: Two faults point the same way. A reporting line through the CEO means bad news about a business line has to pass through the person accountable for that line before it reaches the board - and a warning stopped there leaves no trace that it ever existed. A bonus tied to overall profit puts the CRO on the same side as the people they are meant to supervise. Nobody has to act in bad faith for the system to fail: it fails at the weak, early, uncertain warnings - the most valuable kind - which simply never get raised. This is why the appointment, removal and remuneration of the CRO must sit with the board.

keyTakeaways: The CRO must have a direct line to the board's Risk Committee; appointment and removal sit with the board, not the executive
Three lines of defence: the business owns the risk, the risk function supervises independently, internal audit assures both
The board sets risk appetite; the executive translates it into limits - confusing the two is a governance failure
Disagreement between business and risk is a sign the system is running; what is needed is a pre-written escalation process

summary.keyIdea: The quality of a risk governance framework lies not in the sophistication of the models but in whether the person carrying bad news is able to speak. The reporting line, the appointment power and the escalation process are the three things that decide it.

application.message: When you read a financial institution's annual report, find out who the CRO reports to and how many times a year the Risk Committee meets. Those two details say more about governance health than the whole chapter describing the risk framework.

sections.text: In almost every large collapse, there was a risk function that saw the problem and wrote it down. The question is not why they failed to see it, but why what they saw never reached anywhere that could stop it.
Independence is a structure, not a personal quality

Everyone agrees the risk function must be independent. But independence does not come from hiring someone tough; it comes from that person losing nothing when they say no. If the CRO's pay, bonus and position sit in the hands of the executives running the business, every refusal is a personal bet - and most people place smaller bets as time goes on.
Three lines, and who really owns the risk

The first line is the business unit itself: they create the risk, so they own it. The second line is risk and compliance, supervising independently and setting the framework. The third line is internal audit, checking whether the other two are doing their jobs. The most common misunderstanding is treating the second line as the owner of the risk - at which point the business stops feeling responsible.
The dividing line between board and executive

The board decides how much risk the institution is prepared to take and approves the framework for managing it. The executive translates that statement into limits by division, by desk, by product, and operates within it. When the two roles blur, either the board sinks into operational detail or the executive quietly widens its own appetite.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: One simple and reliable indicator: ask when the risk function last blocked a large transaction. No answer for several years does not mean there was nothing worth blocking.
